content: Acer rubrum, commonly known as the red maple, is one of the most widespread deciduous trees in eastern North America. Its range extends from the Lake of the Woods on the Ontario-Minnesota border, eastward to Newfoundland, southward to near Miami, Florida, and southwestward to eastern Texas. The tree exhibits significant variability in its features, particularly its leaves. At maturity, it typically reaches a height of approximately 25 meters (82 feet). The name red maple is fitting, as its flowers, petioles, twigs, and seeds all display varying shades of red. However, it is most renowned for its striking deep scarlet foliage in autumn. Red maple is highly adaptable to a wide range of site conditions, more so than perhaps any other tree in eastern North America. It thrives in diverse environments, from swamps to dry, poor soils, and nearly everything in between. Elevation is not a limiting factor, as it grows well from sea level to about 900 meters (3,000 feet). Its adaptability and attractive fall foliage make it a popular choice as a shade tree in landscapes. Commercially, it is used on a small scale for maple syrup production and for its medium to high-quality lumber. It is also the state tree of Rhode Island. Description Acer rubrum is a medium to large-sized tree, typically reaching heights of 18 to 27 meters (60 to 90 feet), with exceptional specimens exceeding 35 meters (115 feet). The trunk diameter ranges from 46 to 76 cm (18 to 30 inches), depending on growing conditions. In forests, the bark remains branch-free for a considerable distance up the trunk, while open-grown individuals are shorter and thicker with a more rounded crown. The crown is generally irregularly ovoid, with ascending, whip-like curved shoots. The bark is pale gray and smooth in young trees, darkening and cracking into slightly raised long plates as the tree matures. The leaves are the most distinctive feature for identifying red maple. Like all maples, they are deciduous and arranged oppositely on the twig. They are typically 5–10 cm (2–4 inches) long and wide, with 3–5 palmate lobes and serrated margins. The sinuses are usually narrow, but the leaves can vary significantly. When five lobes are present, the three terminal lobes are larger than the two near the base. The upper side of the leaf is light green, while the underside is whitish and can be glaucous or hairy. The leaf stalks are usually red and up to 10 cm (4 inches) long. In autumn, the leaves turn a brilliant red. The twigs are reddish and somewhat shiny, with small lenticels. The buds are blunt and range in color from greenish to reddish, with several loose scales. The lateral buds are slightly stalked, and collateral buds may also be present. The buds form in fall and winter and are often visible from a distance due to their reddish tint. The flowers are generally unisexual, with male and female flowers appearing in separate sessile clusters, though they can sometimes be bisexual. They emerge in spring, from April to May, usually before the leaves. The tree is considered polygamo-dioecious, meaning some individuals are male, some female, and some monoecious. The flowers are red, with five small petals and a five-lobed calyx, borne in hanging clusters at the twig tips. Pistillate flowers have a single pistil formed from two fused carpels, with a glabrous superior ovary and two long styles that protrude beyond the perianth. Staminate flowers contain 4–12 stamens, often with eight. The fruit is a double samara, 1.5 to 2.5 cm (0.5 to 1 inch) long, with somewhat divergent wings at an angle of 50 to 60 degrees. The samaras are borne on long, slender stems and vary in color from light brown to reddish. They ripen from April through early June, before the leaves are fully developed. Once mature, the seeds are dispersed over a 1–2 week period from April through July. Distribution and Habitat Acer rubrum is one of the most abundant and widespread trees in eastern North America. It ranges from southern Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, and southern Quebec to southwestern Ontario, extreme southeastern Manitoba, and northern Minnesota; southward to Wisconsin, Illinois, Missouri, eastern Oklahoma, and eastern Texas; and eastward to Florida. It has the largest continuous range along the North American Atlantic Coast of any tree that occurs in Florida, spanning 2,575 km (1,600 miles) from north to south. The species is native to all regions of the United States east of the 95th meridian, with three exceptions: the Prairie Peninsula of the Midwest, the coastal prairie in southern Louisiana and southeastern Texas, and the swamp prairie of the Florida Everglades. The absence of red maple in the Prairie Peninsula is particularly notable, as it is not found in the bottomland forests of the Grain Belt, despite being common in similar habitats to the north and south. Its range ends where the -40°C (-40°F) mean minimum isotherm begins, namely in southeastern Canada. The western range is limited by the drier climate of the Great Plains. Nonetheless, red maple has the widest tolerance to climatic conditions of all North American maple species. Its absence in the Prairie Peninsula is likely unrelated to rainfall or other climatic conditions, as it grows well in other locations with comparable or even less annual precipitation. Red maple thrives in a wide range of soil types, with varying textures, moisture levels, pH, and elevations, likely more so than any other forest tree in North America. It grows on both glaciated and non-glaciated soils derived from granite, gneiss, schist, sandstone, shale, slate, conglomerate, quartzite, and limestone. Chlorosis can occur on very alkaline soils, though its pH tolerance is otherwise high. Regarding moisture levels, red maple grows in environments ranging from dry ridges and southwest-facing slopes to peat bogs and swamps. It is commonly found in extreme moisture conditions, both very wet and very dry. While many tree species prefer a specific aspect, such as southor north-facing slopes, red maple does not appear to have a preference. Its ideal conditions are moderately well-drained, moist sites at low or intermediate elevations. However, it is also common in mountainous areas on relatively dry ridges, as well as on both the south and west sides of upper slopes. Additionally, it is frequently found in swampy areas, along the banks of slow-moving streams, and on poorly drained flats and depressions. In northern Michigan and New England, red maple is found on ridge tops, sandy or rocky upland soils, and otherwise dry soils, as well as in nearly pure stands on moist soils and the edges of swamps. In the far south of its range, it is almost exclusively associated with swamps. Interestingly, it is believed that pre-European forests of eastern North America contained far fewer red maples than at present. Most diversity surveys conducted in eastern forests before large-scale exploitation showed red maple representing less than 5% of all tree species, and it was mostly confined to poorly drained areas. The density of red maple in many of these areas has increased sixto sevenfold, and this trend appears to be continuing. A series of disturbances to oak and pine forests since European arrival, such as the suppression of forest fires and global warming, are most likely responsible for this phenomenon. Concerns have been raised, as the ongoing spread of red maple is altering the composition of eastern forests by reducing the number of oaks and pines that would otherwise dominate. Ecology Red maple rarely lives longer than 150 years, making it a shortto medium-lived species. It reaches maturity in 70 to 80 years. Its ability to thrive in a wide variety of habitats is largely due to its capacity to produce roots suited to its site from a young age. In wet locations, red maple seedlings produce short taproots with long and developed lateral roots, while on dry sites, they develop long taproots with significantly shorter laterals. The roots are primarily horizontal, forming in the upper 25 cm (10 inches) of the ground. Mature trees have woody roots up to 25 meters (80 feet) long. They are highly tolerant of flooding, with one study showing that 60 days of flooding caused no leaf damage. At the same time, they are drought-tolerant due to their ability to halt growth under dry conditions and then produce a second growth flush when conditions improve, even if growth has stopped for two weeks. Acer rubrum is one of the first plants to flower in spring. It produces seeds annually, with a bumper crop often occurring every second year. A single tree between 5 and 20 cm (2 and 8 inches) in diameter can produce between 12,000 and 91,000 seeds in a season. Fertilization has been shown to significantly increase seed yield for up to two years after application. The seeds are epigeal and tend to germinate in early summer shortly after they are released, provided there is sufficient light, moisture, and temperature. If the seeds are densely shaded, germination commonly does not occur until the following spring. Most seedlings do not survive in closed forest canopy situations. However, oneto four-year-old seedlings are common under dense canopies, and though they eventually die if no light reaches them, they serve as a reservoir, waiting to fill any open area of the canopy above. Red maple is able to increase its numbers significantly when associate trees are damaged by disease, cutting, or fire. One of its associates, the black cherry (Prunus serotina), contains benzoic acid, which has been shown to be a potential allelopathic inhibitor of red maple growth. Red maple is one of the first species to start stem elongation. In one study, stem elongation was half completed in one week, after which growth slowed and was 90% completed within only 54 days. In good light and moisture conditions, seedlings can grow 30 cm (1 foot) in their first year and up to 60 cm (2 feet) each year for the next few years, making it a fast grower. The red maple serves as a food source for various forms of wildlife. Elk and white-tailed deer, in particular, use the current season's growth of red maple as an important source of winter food. Several Lepidoptera (butterflies and moths) utilize the leaves as food. Toxicity The leaves of red maple, especially when dead or wilted, are highly toxic to horses. The toxin is currently unknown but is believed to be an oxidant, as it destroys red blood cells, causing the blood to be unable to properly transport oxygen—a condition known as acute hemolysis. As little as 1.4 kilograms (3 pounds) of leaves can be lethal. Symptoms appear within one or two days after ingestion and include depression, lethargy, increased breathing rate and depth, increased heart rate, jaundice, dark brown urine, coma, and death. Treatment options are limited and may include the use of methylene blue, mineral oil, and activated carbon to prevent further absorption of the toxin in the stomach. Approximately 50% to 75% of affected horses die or are euthanized as a result. Cultivation Red maple is widely grown as an ornamental tree in parks and large gardens, except where soils are too alkaline or salty. In parts of the Pacific Northwest, it is one of the most common introduced trees. Its popularity in cultivation stems from its vigorous growth habit, attractive and early red flowers, and most importantly, its flaming red fall foliage. The tree was introduced into the United Kingdom in 1656 and shortly thereafter entered cultivation. There, it is frequently found in parks and gardens, as well as occasionally in churchyards. Red maple is a good choice for urban areas when there is ample room for its root system. It is excellent at withstanding harsh urban conditions, including tolerance of both dry and wet soils, and has a higher tolerance of pollution than sugar maple. However, like several other maples, its low root system can be invasive, making it a poor choice for planting in narrow strips between sidewalks and streets. It attracts squirrels, which eat its buds in early spring, although squirrels prefer the larger buds of the silver maple. Cultivars Numerous cultivars have been selected, often for the intensity of fall color, with 'October Glory' and 'Red Sunset' among the most popular. Toward its southern limit, 'Fireburst,' 'Florida Flame,' and 'Gulf Ember' are preferred. Many cultivars of Freeman's Maple (Acer × freemanii) are also widely grown. Examples of cultivars include: 'Armstrong': Columnar to fastigiate in shape with silvery bark and modest orange to red fall foliage. 'Autumn Blaze': Rounded oval form with leaves resembling the silver maple. The fall color is orange-red and persists longer than usual. 'Autumn Flame': A fast grower with exceptionally bright red fall color developing early. The leaves are also smaller than the species. 'October Glory': Rounded oval crown with late-developing intense red fall foliage. It is one of the most popular selections due to its dependable fall color and vigorous growth. Other Uses In the lumber industry, Acer rubrum is considered a soft maple. The wood is close-grained and similar to that of Acer saccharum (sugar maple), but its texture is softer, less dense, and has poorer machining qualities. High grades of red maple wood can nonetheless be substituted for hard maple, particularly in furniture making. As a soft maple, the wood tends to shrink more during the drying process than with hard maples. Red maple is also used for the production of maple syrup, though the hard maples Acer saccharum and Acer nigrum (black maple) are more commonly used. One study compared the sap and syrup from sugar maple with those of red maple, silver maple, boxelder (Acer negundo), and Norway maple (Acer platanoides), and all were found to be equal in sweetness, flavor, and quality. However, the buds of red maple and other soft maples emerge much earlier in the spring than those of sugar maple, and after sprouting, the chemical makeup of the sap changes, imparting an undesirable flavor to the syrup. As a result, red maple can only be tapped for syrup before the buds emerge, making the season very short.
